benchmarks.name: BrowseComp
benchmarks.why_it_matters: Closest proxy here for whether an AI system can dig through the open web to find obscure but verifiable facts.
benchmarks.task_shape: Short-answer questions where the answer is hard to find but easy to verify.
signals: Good fit for backgrounding, source discovery, and hard-to-find fact retrieval.
Not a direct test of source evaluation, narrative synthesis, or interview judgment.

benchmarks.name: GAIA
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A useful benchmark for whether assistants can complete real-world research tasks that require tools and multiple steps.
benchmarks.task_shape: 466 real-world questions with short, unambiguous answers.
signals: Strong signal for agent reliability across mixed research tasks.
Answers are short, so it does not measure explanatory writing or editorial framing.

benchmarks.name: SimpleQA
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A quick signal for whether a model knows when it can answer concise fact questions without inventing.
benchmarks.task_shape: 4,326 short fact-seeking questions with single verifiable answers.
signals: Useful for tracking hallucination risk on factual prompts.
Too narrow for long-form fact checks or reporting memos with many claims.

benchmarks.name: TruthfulQA
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A strong signal for whether a model repeats common falsehoods instead of giving grounded answers.
benchmarks.task_shape: 817 questions across 38 categories designed to elicit imitative falsehoods and popular misconceptions.
signals: Highly relevant to source-sensitive reporting, especially health, law, finance, and politics.
Older benchmark; modern models may be trained against it, so use it alongside newer factuality tests.

benchmarks.name: FEVER
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A foundational benchmark for whether systems can support or refute claims using explicit textual evidence.
benchmarks.task_shape: 185k human-generated claims labeled as supported, refuted, or not enough information, with evidence sentences for supported/refuted claims.
signals: Strong conceptual fit for fact-checking workflows that require evidence, not just an answer.
Evidence is Wikipedia-based, so it does not capture the messiness of primary documents, local records, or reporting notes.

benchmarks.name: MMLU
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A broad general-capability signal for whether a model has baseline knowledge across domains reporters often touch.
benchmarks.task_shape: Multiple-choice questions across 57 academic and professional subjects.
signals: Useful as a broad sanity check for general knowledge and problem solving.
Less close to newsroom work because it is multiple-choice and often saturated by frontier models.

benchmarks.name: TableBench
benchmarks.why_it_matters: Directly overlaps with common reporting work: ask questions of tables, compare numbers, and reason from structured data.
benchmarks.task_shape: 886 curated test cases across fact checking, numerical reasoning, data analysis, and visualization.
signals: High relevance to spreadsheets, agency data, and published tables.
Small enough that individual task coverage matters; inspect examples before over-weighting scores.

benchmarks.name: BIRD-SQL
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A practical signal for whether models can turn plain-English questions into SQL over realistic, messy databases.
benchmarks.task_shape: 12,751 question-SQL pairs over 95 large databases totaling 33.4 GB across 37 professional domains.
signals: Highly relevant to querying public records, enterprise databases, and structured investigative datasets.
Scores can depend on schema linking, retrieval, and hand-provided domain evidence, so raw model comparisons need context.

benchmarks.name: DocIE
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A close fit for turning large unstructured document dumps into entities, mentions, types, and relationships.
benchmarks.task_shape: Systems process long unstructured documents and output entity mention clusters, entity types, and relation triples.
signals: Strong match for document-dump triage, entity lists, relationship mapping, and building structured leads from text.
The benchmark is newer and challenging; baseline scores are low, so treat it as a frontier capability signal rather than a mature production benchmark.

benchmarks.name: IDP Leaderboard
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A practical benchmark family for extracting fields, classifying documents, reading long files, and handling visually structured PDFs.
benchmarks.task_shape: A unified leaderboard across intelligent document processing tasks including KIE, OCR, VQA, document classification, long-document processing, table extraction, and confidence scoring.
signals: Very relevant to PDFs, scanned records, forms, filings, contracts, invoices, and large document sets.
It mixes several document-processing tasks, so compare rows within the same IDP sub-benchmark rather than across all IDP tasks.

benchmarks.name: ChartQA
benchmarks.why_it_matters: Tests whether vision-language models can answer questions about charts rather than only describe them.
benchmarks.task_shape: Human-written and generated questions over charts, emphasizing visual and logical reasoning.
signals: Useful for auditing chart interpretation in multimodal models.
Chart screenshots are cleaner than many real newsroom source documents.

benchmarks.name: TAT-QA
benchmarks.why_it_matters: Good proxy for annual reports, budgets, filings, and other reporting materials where tables and prose must be read together.
benchmarks.task_shape: 16,552 questions over 2,757 hybrid table-text contexts from financial reports.
signals: Strong match for financial and accountability reporting workflows.
Domain is finance-heavy, so it may miss messier civic-data formats.

benchmarks.name: TabFact
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A direct fit for checking whether a claim is supported or contradicted by structured data.
benchmarks.task_shape: 118k human-annotated statements using 16k Wikipedia tables as evidence.
signals: Useful lens for table-backed fact checks.
Binary entail/refute labels simplify the messier reality of journalistic evidence.

benchmarks.name: DS-1000
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A practical benchmark for whether models can help write and repair everyday Python analysis code.
benchmarks.task_shape: 1,000 data science coding problems spanning seven Python libraries.
signals: Strong overlap with computational reporting notebooks.
Does not evaluate data cleaning judgment, provenance, or statistical interpretation.

benchmarks.name: DA-Code
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A close proxy for whether an AI system can autonomously explore real datasets, write analysis code, and derive answers from messy data.
benchmarks.task_shape: 500 complex real-world data analysis tasks across data wrangling, exploratory analysis, and machine learning in an executable environment.
signals: Stronger fit than short coding tests for notebook-style reporting workflows that require planning, iteration, and data inspection.
Still evaluates task completion in a benchmark harness, so it does not fully capture editorial judgment, source provenance, or whether the analysis question was the right one.

benchmarks.name: SWE-bench
benchmarks.why_it_matters: A useful signal for whether AI coding agents can debug real projects rather than only write short snippets.
benchmarks.task_shape: Real GitHub issues where a model must generate a patch that resolves the described problem.
signals: Strong proxy for maintaining data pipelines, scrapers, parsers, and newsroom analysis tools.
Not specific to pandas or R, and scores can depend heavily on the agent scaffold around the model.
